Mr. Coric requested for those men to be returned to him, and I believe that for a little while longer the situation remained unchanged until it was clear that the offensive had been crushed, and then the order on the resubordination of the military police had been -- was made null and void.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I had already said how surprised I was after looking at the document because of the number of victims, seeing the number of military police. There were a lot of casualties, people killed or wounded, and I had tried to understand why, and one of the answers had been at the time that they were in combat unity -- units, combat units, and I think I remember a witness told us, I don't know his name, that the military police was well equipped, well trained, and that therefore they were quite operational in combat, which explained why many of them were killed. Now, yourself as commander of the HVO from July to November, did you feel that this corps of military policemen was particularly vulnerable because of its casualties in combat?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police was well equipped. They were great fighters. The military policemen were a select few, in actual fact, as fighters, and they fought very well. And frequently because they were so well organised they would take it upon themselves to do the toughest jobs if -- in defence. Many people were killed. We had a lot of casualties. And the people who fought most were killed most often, and among those who fought well there were some military police battalions, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As you know, Mr. Coric was -- became minister of interior. He was appointed as minister of interior on the 20th of November, 1993, while you were no more in your post. Did this seem to you to be a normal appointment or a promotion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt about that two or three months later probably, because I went back to all the great jobs that I had to do in Zagreb, and I was no longer versed in the appointments, in fact, of the appointments in Herceg-Bosna. I knew that a new team had arrived. I knew that the data processing continued about anything that was contrary to the law or outside the law, and I know that this bore fruit at the beginning of 1994 when in Rama, Prozor, 27 people were arrested, because I went back in January at the invitation of some of my guys to help out. But to be quite frank, I didn't know for a long time that the minister of the interior was Valentin Coric. But had I known, that would have been quite a normal appointment judging by all the facts that I knew about. At that point in time that would have been fight normal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let's speak about Mr. Pusic, Berislav. When did you meet Mr. Pusic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as to Mr. Pusic from the war and after the war, I can't tell you anything because I never actually met him. There were at least seven or eight people with the surname Pusic that I had heard about, and I knew that there was this man called Berislav Pusic, but I only met him, I think, in 2004, before we set out for the Hague. And each year, at least twice a year, they would say, "Yes, he's going to The Hague. There's a secret indictment raised." That happened at least twice a year six or seven years before the year 2004. And then one day in 2004 the indictment arrived for five people, five individuals, and I could count the five but I didn't know who the sixth one was. And then I called up the minister of justice. I knew her because she was an advisor in President Tudjman's office. I asked her who is the sixth man, and she said it's Berislav Pusic. And then I asked around for a telephone number so I could inform him, because I thought this would be a surprise to him. Well, it was a surprise for all of us, but for him too. And I happened to find him in hospital. He was in Ljubljana, lying in hospital after an operation, and he said -- and I said, "Listen. So that they don't arrest you as you fugitive, if you're at all able, and even in a wheelchair, come to Zagreb and give yourself up like the rest of us did." And that's all I know about Berislav Pusic, except for the prison term, and I can have course tell you another story about our life in prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a specific organ in charge of exchanging prisoners, finding people. Did you know or did you not know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know that there was a service for the exchange of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you didn't know that Mr. Pusic was one of the persons responsible for this, in charge?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was another name that was bandied about, but I can't be sure now. I didn't know who was in charge of all that. I did know that the service existed, but nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. So now we are going to talk about somebody else who is in the indictment. It is Mr. Blaskic, who is quoted as a member of this enterprise in which you and your comrades are -- who are present and who -- the Croatian people were responsible, and who have died. First of all, let's speak about Blaskic. When did you get acquainted with him? When did you meet him? At what date did you meet Tihomir Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him in 1992, several days after the fall of Jajce. And Jajce fell on the 28th or 9th. Yes, the 28th or 9th. Of October [as interpreted], was it, 1993? Now, two days after the fall of Jajce, or perhaps three days after the fall of Jajce, but at any rate several days after the fall of Jajce I managed to break through --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I apologise for the interruption. Our transcript indicates that the witness said that the fall of Jajce was in October of 1993, and I don't know whether he intended to say that or whether that's just a mistake in the translation. Perhaps he could clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak. What is the date of the fall of Jajce?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 1992, actually. The date is okay, but the year was wrong. 1992. And I don't know, two or three after the fall of Jajce, I can't say for certain, but I managed to break through and reach Tihomir Blaskic, and I found him in a room in a building. And Mr. Filipovic was up there too. And it was a situation of war. The Serbs were bombing Travnik heavily. There was a lot of shooting. And I asked what the situation was like, where the front lines were. I said, "When do you expect the Serbs to attack Travnik?" And -- well, I could go on and on and tell you a great deal about that, what it was like and so forth and how long I stayed there and what I did and so on. I knew a young man there. I talked to him. I got to know him better later on. He was in the Yugoslav People's Army. He was the commander of a battalion, an infantry battalion, I assume, in Slovenia. And when the war broke out in Slovenia, he escaped. He fled to Austria, because I think had he had a wife -- his wife had some family there. So he didn't join in the war in Croatia, but he did come in -- well, he came to his local area where he was born. He was born up there, and he placed himself at the disposal of the HVO. And so people who had started organising the resistance earlier, they were a little suspicious why he had come in so late, what he was doing in Austria, and I had to stifle those rumours, because he was an officer, judging by everything that I could see, who knew what he was about. He knew his business. But the job he knew as an officer in the JNA was not sufficient for him to be able to organise the defence of Travnik, because in fact he didn't have an army to work with. And if somebody came, then they also escaped and fled. So in other words, I was a self-appointed person. And when I saw that there was nobody --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting, Mr. Praljak. You're all the time now 18 lines long talking about a young man. Would you be able to identify that person? On page 51, line 25 you say I knew a young man there, and then it looks as if you're always talking about this young man. Who is that? Is that Mr. Tihomir Blaskic or ...

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the young man Mlad Covjek, is a little older than a young man, but actually I'm referring to a young man, not a young guy, a youngster, Mlad in Croatian and then young man, but yes the young man I'm referring to is Tihomir Blaskic, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are talking about him because he was born on the 2nd of December, 1960. You were born in 1945. So in your eyes he was a young man at the time. In 1992 he was 32 years old.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he looked young to me. He looked like a young man to me. I didn't know when he was born, so he looked younger, because 16 years is quite an age difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the end of 1992, what post did he have in the military as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander of the operative zone of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, could you give me the names of the other commanders of the other operational zones. For the one in Vitez, for instance, in Rasa [phoen]. Can you give us these names?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blaskic was the commander of the operative zone, which included Travnik, Novi Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca, Kiseljak, Vares. So he was the commander of this whole operational zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who were the other commanders of the other operational zones?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the commander of the operation zone of North-east Herzegovina was Siljeg, as far as I remember. And then you had the South-western zone of Mostar, and that was Mico Lasic at the time. What did you say? What? Well, if Petkovic denies that --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll just put right some names of the zone. North-western Herzegovina was Siljeg, and the south-eastern zone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ah, yes, that's right. I mix that all up, yes. South-east Herzegovina was Lasic, north-west was Siljeg, Central Bosnia was Blaskic, and Posavina, Matuzovic. Djuro Matuzovic. I think I've got it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know that Colonel Blaskic was tried for the facts he was charged with. He was not a member of the joint criminal enterprise. This was mentioned in your indictment. This young man, Colonel Blaskic, did you have political discussions with him or was your relationship purely military, you didn't know what his thoughts were on political issues?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to the man about many things, because in a way I had to raise his authority in the area. Although the topics were mostly military with respect to organisation, military discipline, and so on and so forth, many things with respect to units that were not obedient, and so on, and how to rectify that, but I also discussed political issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was his view of the situation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, no -- we had no differences of views. The man never said an ugly word about Muslims. He never uttered any bad words about anybody. Not about the Serbs or about anybody else. He was a real soldier. And I spent a lot of time with Mr. Jaganjac and with others to try and set up a joint command with the BH Army, and I went regularly to visit the headquarters and commanders of the BH Army in the area, and Blaskic went with me, and we had dozens of discussions discussing the topic with officers from the BH Army as well, and I was given the stamps and seals. And both sides recognised me, especially since we managed to defend Travnik successfully, given me certain rights, although let me repeat that I was a self-appointed man over there. In a way, I raised myself up to a level to something -- well, I was appointed to the commission - what was it? - to mediate between Alija Izetbegovic and Franjo Tudjman or the joint board or council as it was called. But quite simply in Travnik, after the fall of Jajce, there was nobody there who knew that the town had been so disrupted, and the BH Army, except for one unit by -- under Mr. Leka in Turbe had nothing, possessed nothing. So somebody had to step in. And now what could I do, either get in my car and go home or the Serbs would reach Sarajevo. So then you take over and begin issuing orders, and then they obey you so you issue some more orders and one thing leads to another, Your Honours. That's the gist of it very frankly and sincerely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going to spend a lot of time on Colonel Blaskic, but as -- I have a short question. Have you read the judgement handed down in the Colonel Blaskic case? Have you read the -- both judgements?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the first-instance judgement, but I learned about the second-instance judgement -- well, just come details, but I did read the first-instance judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've read the judgement, and the first one handed down by the Trial Chamber, the second one handed down by the Appeals Chamber. What about Ahmici? Where were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you were not involved in Ahmici. You know what Colonel Blaskic was charged with. He was charged with what happened, amongst other things, in Ahmici. In the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution, which you have not read, it is stated in paragraph 65 -- I shall read it out to you. It's very short. It says the following: "On the 19th of January at 00.30, the HVO launched offensive against the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and has burnt several Muslim villages in the area," paragraph 379 of the Blaskic judgement. According to the Prosecution, it seems that Ahmici was part of the HVO attack. The Appeals Chamber corrected somewhat -- no, corrected the view adopted by the Trial Chamber as stating that as far as it was concerned, Ahmici was a target where ABiH men may have been stationed. The Appeals Chamber says that there was fighting between both sides, and the Appeals Chamber does not take a very clear stance on who was attacking and who was defending its positions. When you learnt what had happened in Ahmici, how did you react?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had a twofold reaction. First of all, I was shocked. And secondly, I was a little skeptical whether it was actually how -- it happened actually how the Bosnian and world media reported it, because I found during the war and after the war that there was a vast quantity of lies and tricks played in that war, deceit and so on. And we've heard everything about Stupni Dol, and I simply -- well, nobody could convince me that you can find in that small village 15 victims, and they say in the documents that ten soldiers were killed, and that then somebody sits over there and for another four months without any investigation and inquiry receives information from someone in the BH Army telling him that the man died in Stupni Dol. So nobody carried out any quality inquiry or investigation. And it's difficult to understand how the people burnt in those houses were burnt in those houses. Who did that with what purpose in mind. And the HVO in the morning carried out the action, and it was no longer there in the afternoon. So there was no investigation into the truth. It was a propaganda war of enormous proportion. Today, Your Honours, we are having books written, books are being published from the international circles. The Americans are writing books who were in the secret services previously, and they say how many -- what propaganda did, the kind of job it did which had nothing to do with the truth and I was shocked, that's my first reaction; and secondly, I found it difficult to accept that that's actually what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, have you been to Stupni Dol?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: On -- on what, then, do you base your affirmation that it was such a small place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we saw here every single house on every single photograph. I think we saw at least 15 photographs from Stupni Dol and we looked at every angle and every house there, every trench, every little pathway. And then they speak about buildings destroyed. There is no rubble or destroyed houses. And then it says that there were these cellars. Then it says that there were unarmed people, whereas they themselves say that there were ten soldiers, and then a hundred people from international organisations come in and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I asked a very short question and you have answered that. Now, a second short question: How many houses are there in Stupni Dol? Can you just give the number of the houses there? If you looked at it so carefully, you certainly know, approximately. Five, ten, 20?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's 40 houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, then I don't know why you wonder that 15 bodies could be found. If there are 40 houses, there may have been four to ten people living in a house. Why do you say that it's so unbelievably much to find in such a village 15 bodies? I do not quite understand the logic of your argument.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think you understood me properly, Your Honour. If in a village three teams from the international community with investigators enter it, and if there are 40 houses and if they stay there the whole day, if they spend the whole day there and then they come up and find 15 bodies, dead bodies, and over a space of three or four months we have 38 bodies, what were those people doing there? There might have been ten people in the houses. Then this would make it 300 bodies. That's precisely what I'm saying. The investigation was conducted in a catastrophic manner. We can say they found 15 bodies and that concluded the investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have answered my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I will now address the case of Dario Kordic who was also perhaps a young man since he was born on the 14th of December, 1960 in Sarajevo. In what circumstances did you meet Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same time I met Blaskic I met Kordic, but I met Kordic far more superficially. Perhaps at two meetings, brief ones, so that -- and I also got to know him. I met him in the film when that brigade in Zenica was being established, where he delivered some sort of speech. And I told them not to smoke while they were standing to attention. And I don't remember when I met Dario Kordic after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you didn't see him very often.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A maximum number of three times, let's say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you have political conversations with him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a brief the political discussion. I did have that with him. And I remember my comments. Those political speeches were not anything that I could object to and criticise, but I told him to cut the rhetoric a bit, cut down on the rhetoric. In other words, I said, "Dario, listen here. Reduce the rhetoric a bit." So in translation, that would mean don't be so passionate in delivering your speeches. I remember me telling him that once. I'm referring to the speech in Zenica, in actual fact, not speeches generally but the speech in Zenica, I think. Well, he was raising, boosting morale with the people he had to work with. You had to boost their morale, and everybody had to be passionate in boosting morale, because -- well, what I want to tell you, Your Honours, the Serbs after Jajce were going straight towards Travnik and from thence on to Sarajevo. And when I sent Blaskic to gather together some planks and shovels and find some volunteers and go to arrange places to help dig trenches, these people asked him for certificates and receipts for, say, half a cubic metre of planks, whereas the director of the factory, the manager of the factory said, "Well, why are you waking me up at 2.00 a.m.? Do you know what the time is? It's 2.00 a.m." So it's impossible to understand things without entering into the psychology of the people there. They were laid back. There was war on their threshold and they weren't realising it. And since it hadn't reached their threshold yet, they were like ostriches with their heads in the sand expecting the storm to pass. And so quite literally you had to kick them in the ass and wake them up or some other way or get hold of the most important ones by their heads and unleash this mechanism of raising their psychological morale and level so that they were ready to fight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even if you only met Kordic on a few occasions, you knew his personality. When he was vice-president of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did this come as a surprise to you or not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't know that he had taken up that position. I met a person sporting spectacles, clumsy, God-fearing person, and when I heard that he was charged with crimes, it was not a surprise to me based on the impression that I had of him. That person, according to what I saw, was a very devout Catholic, and to this very day it remains a sheer enigma to me how to reconcile what I'd seen up there and the accusations against that person as capable of ordering crimes. I'm not going to prejudice anything, but this is still a dilemma, something that I'm really not clear on, but the times were difficult. It was war. Everybody can -- well, I'm just telling you what my impression was about a practising Christian who believed in the ten commandments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: An observation regarding the transcript -- [B/C/S interpretation on English channel]. UNIDENTIFIED SPEAKER: [Interpretation] Being showy, I quite like the understated but great quality aspect.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think it was line 23, 24 -- 24 of page 60. "When I heard that he was charged with crimes, it was not a surprise to me based on the impression I had of him." I wonder whether that is really what you wanted to say or the opposite.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite the opposite. Base on the impression that I had during our several meetings, I saw that he was a practising Catholic, that he believed in the ten commandments, and it really came as a major surprise to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That brings this sentence into line with the rest of what you have stated. Please continue, or whoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going to press the point as regards Dario Kordic. There's something which seems much more important to me, and that is the case of Naletilic, Tuta. Can you tell me when you met him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In childhood. He hails from Siroki Brijeg. He is two years my junior, I believe. Siroki Brijeg is a very small place. There were not that many of us there. All the children knew each other, and that's when I got to know Mladen Naletilic. In 1961 I left Siroki Brijeg, and the next time I saw Tuta Naletilic was in 1992. He had been to Sarajevo, and after that he emigrated abroad and so on and so forth. What I'm saying is that I knew him in the 1960s, and then I met him again in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as his political views were concerned, did he have any particular views or didn't he? What was your impression of him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the 1990s -- or, rather, in 1992 when I met him down there, he had already met some lads in Siroki Brijeg -- or, rather, some units. Even before that, of course. There were some excellent guys among them, some splendid guys. However, one thing is true. Mr. Naletilic does not respect order. He is willing to respect order as long as it is his order, and he wanted his units to be apart from anybody else and for him to occupy a very special place. That's for one. Second of all, as far as the political views are concerned, he definitely belonged to the political circles which perceived Muslims as brethren and even more than that, and this derived from the independent states of Croatia, and even before that when Muslims were treated as Croats of Muslim religion. And according to such theories, they were considered a flower of the Croatian nation, as the healthiest, the best segment of the Croatian people according to that line of thought. That's what Muslims were for them. And it is certain that in 1992, and in one part of 1993, Mladen Naletilic Tuta advocated such similar ideas. After that, up to the event that we have already discussed here, I did not have much contact with him. I don't remember having had any contact with him. And after that incident we did not have any contact at all until the moment of imprisonment. At one point we did bump into each other. He started apologising to me, and then I said, "Well, you could have done --" but let me not go into that. After the incident that we discussed, I never had any more contact with him. I didn't want to have any more contact with him. I did not consider him as somebody under my command and he was never under my command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. We shall now come to this. You said Siroki Brijeg he constituted a unit. This battalion, this battalion of sentenced convicts --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were two. One was called the Convicts Battalion and the other was called the Anti-Terrorist Battalion or something like that. So there were two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: One was a regular one led by Mr. Andabak first, and then later by Mr. Lija. What was his surname? Mandic. And that one was a good regular unit. As for the other one and what happened with it and around it, to be quite frank I don't know. I can't say. But I always got the names mixed up of these two, what was one, what was the other. Anyway, I'm talking about the unit -- the good unit that was commanded by Andabak, one of the Andabaks, and then later on it was commanded by Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say he wasn't under your authority. How was it possible?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it simply was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please explain.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not want to issue any orders to him. In my view he was not part of the system. I did not represent anything to him. I could not do anything to him. He was not part of my system. He was not under my command. The only thing I could do was to raise a brigade, step out of my authorities, and do what I was not authorised to do, take the area militarily. That was not my job. That was not my problem. That is something I said loud and clear to Mate Boban, and everybody knew that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall now go to the heart-of-hearts of the question. On the 5th of May, according to the Prosecution's argument, which is developed in the indictment and in the preliminary, the Muslims are arrested on the 5th of May, and it is Naletilic who is going to arrest these people. People are going to be taken first to the stadium, later to the Heliodrom. In the Naletilic judgement all this is described in great detail. On the 5th of May, where are you? Yes. The 9th of May, excuse me. On the 9th of May, where are you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure I was not in Mostar. Whether I was in Zagreb, whether I was on the road, I don't know, but I'm sure I was not in Mostar. It's a hundred percent fact. Whether I was in Zagreb, whether I was travelling, I can't really tell you with any degree of certainty. I'm sure that I arrived on the 11th in the morning. That's when I arrived in Mostar, and I told you everything exactly as it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your admissions, you described the -- you say that for the events of the 9th of May you were not at all implicated.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll just take the case in which what you say is true, you are not implicated in anything which has happened or is happening. On the 9th of May, we have heard and you have heard of victims tell us that they were arrested, transferred to the stadium and then to the Heliodrom. This you have heard, just as I have. How can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, later on on the 11th, what happened happened. I left. I pulled over on the curb, but I left. However, from a conversation with the lads on the bus, or a couple of buses, that I took to the church for the service and so on and so forth, from my conversation with Mico Lasic and the commanders whom I'd known from before, I explicitly asked them who was it who launched the attack first. And nobody would have lied to me at the moment. It was not the HVO that launched the attack. They were not the first to attack. There were plans, and later on you saw them as seized material in Vranica. The Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was preparing for an attack, and that attack was launched on the 9th, and that's all I know. Secondly, there were two things. When fighting starts in a city -- and I'm talking just hypothetically as if I had been there. When fighting starts in a city and when you cannot establish where the line begins or ends, then you are not in a position to know who your enemy in the surrounding buildings is, because they're shooting from the windows, from the roofs, and so on and so forth. I personally believe that in such situations it is admissible and it is possible to take a group of people from the area but not ethnically segregated and to move them from the area until the situation is resolved. However, the treatment of the people in question had to be in compliance with the conventions. And that's my opinion. I believe that this is admissible. I did it in Vakuf because there were civilians in a war zone and I was responsible for their lives. And then I said, "You're going to take these people together with their cows, and you will move them to a different place." And then I appoint a person and say, "You will be held responsible for this and that and the other." This is admissible. I don't know if this is admissible under law. However, in my head, in my heart, it is admissible. This should be admissible. However, in such a situation it really matters what you're going to do with that -- with those people next. This is my hypothetical view. I don't know what happened. I heard subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we get into what you've just mentioned, that is that persons were captured who were in an area where there had been some shots, you know just as well as I do, and you said yourself a few days ago and that struck me, you said to the Judges, I'm quoting you word-for-word, "For me the best defence is to say the truth." This is what you told us. So now continue [microphone not activated] say. Now you're telling us the truth, and we know that hundreds of people were arrested. We know that several buses were needed to take them to the place. Therefore, there was an operation on. According to you, if Mr. Naletilic directed this operation at that precise moment on the 9th of May, he was under the orders of whom? Under whose orders was he acting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer your question, Your Honour. I offered what I said previously by way of a hypothesis. This could have been ordered only by Mico Lasic, certainly not by Mr. Naletilic Tuta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to put you in a difficult position, but now we are talking about a particularly military problem. We have soldiers from the HVO who arrest people. We'll have to determine whether these arrests were illicit or not. That's another problem. I'm not examining this aspect. All I simply wish to know is that within the framework of the military operation, the soldiers of Naletilic were under the authority of Naletilic, of course, no problem, but Naletilic himself was under the authority of whom?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honours. At the time, I did not have a function down there. I knew who the chief of the Main Staff was. It was Petkovic, but he was not in the area. I know that I arrived on the 11th. I told you what had happened. I don't know. It is true in my view honesty is the best policy and that the truth is the best defence, and I'm telling you what I'm telling you. I can't tell you what I don't know because I don't know, but I also said this: If I'd been in charge of the operation, maybe I would have taken into account people's safety, and I would have done what I did in Vakuf, and this would have depended on my assessment whether the civilians would start dying, but the implementation would have been different. I'm not talking about any numbers, about buses. I'm just offering my hypothesis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to be directive in my questions. I don't want to be leading, so I'm trying to stick mostly to technical and military aspects. An operation which consists in taking people from point A to put them in point B and then a place C, one being the stadium then the Heliodrom, C being the Heliodrom, this is an operation where there are several people who are involved in this operation. On the military plane, should this be before, and I'm saying -- insisting on before? Has this been planned, organised? Just a little detail. The buses, this is not just by clapping your hands that you can have eight buses within seconds. You need petrol. You need drivers. You must give them a timetable. So militarily speaking -- according to you, you're a specialist, you had a high post in the military. Doesn't this imply a minimum of planning, organisation, logistics?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way that you have just put it, Judge Antonetti, I would say yes, but I don't know when it started, at what time. I don't know when people were taken. I don't know when the buses came. There were buses in Mostar that used to take children and civilians out of Mostar. One would have to look at the schedule to see when the operation started, when the fire broke out, where the buses were, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. So we have two hypotheses, two assumptions, working assumptions or hypotheses. We did not discuss between ourselves, Judges, so we don't know what the conclusions are. The two hypotheses, you just know them as well as I do. The first one is the Prosecutor, the attack of HVO, and the consequences, Muslims are arrested and so on. Second hypothesis, working hypothesis, an offensive of the BiH, a defence from the HVO, and within this defence framework, one, we doesn't know who is one [as interpreted], considers that it is necessary to arrest Muslims. This is the second hypothesis. But then if in this second hypothesis it is decided to arrest Muslims, who is in a position to give the order? Is it Mr. Naletilic? Is it the commander the operational zone, Mr. Petkovic who isn't there? The authorities, civilian authorities of the HVO? Mr. Prlic? But Mr. Prlic, we know that he was [indiscernible] Makarska on that day. Mr. Boban, in person, who would have had a direct connection with Naletilic without asking Petkovic and Lasic ? How do you analyse this situation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will share with you what I think. From what I learnt subsequently in my conversations with the commanders, with the commander of the Ljubuski brigade, Tomic and Commander Lasic, the commander of the operational zone, the commander of the 2nd Brigade whom I'd asked, for example, "Okay, Tomic, were you scheduled to be engaged in an attack in Mostar?" And he said, "No. I was summoned subsequently." In other words, according to all the information that I have and that I stick to, the HVO had not planned any attacks. Your Honour, if you are to attack Mostar, if you are to attack any city, it cannot be done without Boban, without Petkovic, without Lasic. It just cannot be done. The evening before there were a lot of people from the international community because there had been some meetings. This is what I heard here, actually. In my view, after the attack of the BH Army, and you could see in Hadziosmanovic's book that Muslims defected to our side, their infantry, and I'm just speaking hypothetically. Most probably there was panic and in that state of panic Naletilic Tuta thought that it was his right, but I'm again speaking hypothetically about an event that I did not -- I wasn't involved. Most often the response is hysterical. People are arrested, you start shooted in people's backs [as interpreted]. And this is a very plausible course of events, because the border was in the western part of Mostar. That's where the command was. And little by little they start occupying small chunks of areas without ever having fought against the Chetniks. The animosity that was the result of that was already there. And then when there is an attack, people start behaving in an extremist way. They start cursing each other. They start mentioning their mothers, talking about back-stabbing. And then the situation can escalate, and then the situation is taken over by somebody who hasn't any right to do so, and then they pursue their own policy and they wage their own war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. So to these very precise questions I have asked you, you have no answer, because you don't know whether there was some planning or certain orders, but admitting what you say, is it possible for a military commander of the level of Naletilic could behind his command, his hierarchy, behind the authorities, arrest women, children, elderly people, adults, adult men and have them incarcerated or provisionally kept in a place? We can use several words or expressions to qualify what happened. Is it possible for an individual just under his own steam just decide everything? This is what I'm trying to understand.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm saying it loud and clear: Yes. Naletilic could do that. He was outside of any systems. He was not under anybody's control. You saw what happened on the 11th. Mr. Valentin Coric was at that meeting, and so was the head of the SIS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to tell you that --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... anything to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to tell you, General Praljak, but I've already said so but I will tell you again so that you remember, that there was a document, unfortunately I haven't taken it now, and in this document there is a report made by a military policeman who writes very clearly that Tuta's men were doing ethnical cleansing, and this report was sent upwards in the military police. So clearly if this document says what the writer was saying, it shows at least that some military policemen did not take part in this operation, and this is rather troubling. But on the other hand, there have been some casualties. The victims have explained to us that some policemen came into their house, flat, and evicted them and so on. So we also have that. Therefore, it's a sort of mosaic of testimonies that are very diverse. You know that the Spanish have filmed the column, and we saw this video, after which these people were put in the Heliodrom. There problems occurred to feed them, to house them and so on. Now you tell me that you heard about this on the 11th of November. Sorry, the 11th of May, 11th of May. When you heard about this on the 11th of May, did you intervene to say some people are in the Heliodrom and have no reason to be there? What did you do at your own level about this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the 11th I just learnt about the part of that. I was at the meeting which ended the way it did, and what I'm saying is this -- let's understand one thing. There weren't that many people in the room. There was Mr. Valentin Coric and the head of the SIS in charge of security, and what was happening to me was what was happening, and I am telling you honestly and sincerely. At that moment, Mr. Valentin Coric -- or Mr. Coric were not able to bring Mr. Naletilic Tuta to any order. And it's a fact. He was just too powerful, too strong. He had his team of people. And this could have been done only if one had taken 300 men and started a showdown with him or -- with an intent to kill him. And it is nothing out of the ordinary. In the Vietnam War, for example, there were people who were mavericks, who were renegades, and then one had to wait for your power to grow to the extent to be able to overcome such power. That's the first thing. Secondly, that problem started being dealt with on the 12th. On the 11th and on the 12th I spoke to Mr. Sefko Omerbasic who was the president of the Meshihat of the Islamic community in Zagreb in Croatia. The two of us together went to the Spanish Bat. Mr. Petkovic had returned as well, and we started elucidating that problem. I was not the one who was directly involved in that. I was involved through the conversations at the higher level, and that problem was resolved relatively fast. I'm speaking based on the documents that I've seen here. A cease-fire was signed when Halilovic came, when Petkovic came, and that's how it all ended. And then I tried to put the whole situation under a certain level of control based on my conversations which Sefko Omerbasic, Petkovic, and UNPROFOR. And again before the 30th of June we had a cease-fire the way it was. And that would be my very correct, very precise answer to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few figures before breaking. In paragraph 45 about Naletilic, it seems that on that day there was 1.500 to 2.000 civilians who were Muslims who were arrested and taken to the Heliodrom. Between 1.500 and 2.000. You see this figure. The Prosecution, in its filings, also tells us that there was a list of the arrested people in three categories, women, children, and elderly. Listen to these figures. 216 women, 216; 104 children, 104 children; 31 elderly people. So what is staring us in the face is the 104 children. How can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, and Judges, hypothetically I'll give you an answer because you're asking me something -- you're asking me to explain something which -- well, I don't know how. Let's assume that I'm planning an attack in Mostar and that I expect a terrible or sufficiently great pounding at the houses or in streets behind me. So I would take out women, children, and elderly men. How are you going to leave the children if that's it? And I'm speaking hypothetically. In Capljina, for example, because of sniper fire from some of the flats I asked that the blinds be lowered, and I asked that people be taken out of the flats that were facing the Serb artillery to the parts of the building that were further away and less likely to be hit by shells, and then I asked that women, children, and men and the elderly do that. So how am I going to transfer the men and leave the children to be killed? I don't know what the reason was here or the motive, and I don't want to enter into that. I can't into that [as interpreted]. But what I'm saying is -- well, the situation when in Gornji Vakuf, I moved the people with the cows and all the rest of their goods and chattels. I'm not going to leave the children. I took care of them. I moved them out because I felt this to be necessary. I don't know how else to put it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under oath you are saying that you knew nothing about the fact that there were a hundred children in the Heliodrom. You're saying that you didn't know this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On oath I'm telling you that I knew none of this information. I didn't know it on the 11th. I only learnt about it later on. On the 11th I was completely beside myself and left the meeting in that state and went further on. I had nothing to do there. There was nothing for me to do there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the break I would put any more questions. I have just one additional question on Doljani and Sovici. We shall now have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. I believe that you would like to say something, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Just a brief matter. Today is the due date of the Prosecution response to a motion filed by the Prlic Defence to reopen its case, and it's a motion that was also joined, I believe, by the Praljak Defence. Today is our due date for filing the response. I just was informed over the break the response is -- is ready to be filed. Apparently it was just as it was getting ready to be filed it was discovered that it was about 500 words over the limit, the word limit. It's only at about nine pages, but for whatever reason it's 500 words over the limit, and we're asking an order to enable us to -- to get this filed now. And I've conferred with the Prlic Defence about this, so we're asking for permission to file -- go ahead and file the response now with it being 500 words over the limit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has conferred and grants you permission for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, indeed. Mr. Praljak, still talking about the 9th of May and then the 11th of May. Do you know who was in charge of Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could it be that Naletilic was the commander of Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judge Trechsel, Your Honour, I can't give you any information in that regard, because as you well know, on the 30th of April, in the Croatian parliament, I managed to get a delegation to go and calm the situation down there, and then afterwards I agreed with Mr. Sefko Omerbasic that we go down there together, and that he should talk to the eastern side and that they try and calm the conflict down. I had no authority, no authorisation, and I gave you an hour-by-hour account of what I did at that time, so I have absolutely no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: On the 11th, during that meeting, did you or anyone else suggest, was the subject at all discussed, that the persons who had been arrested and were still at Heliodrom be immediately released?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judge Trechsel, Your Honour, as far as I'm concern the meeting ended in the space of ten minutes. There was no question of any information that is mentioned here. There wasn't discussion about anything. I advocated peace. The person to whom we spoke and we spoke about reacted in the way he did and I left the meeting. I stopped at a curve, asked a young guy to let the UNPROFOR pass, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If you -- from the moment you have left the meeting you are not expected to say what -- what happened. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I shall finish putting my questions about Naletilic by discussing events that occurred in Sovici and Doljani on the 17th of April, 1993. This is my first question: On the 17th of April, 1993, where were you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, Your Honour. I don't know where I was exactly on the 17th of April, whether I was in Zagreb or perhaps in Mostar. So what the exact day it was when with Arif Pasalic I found myself on the east bank with respect to the events, I can't say just now, but what I can say under three oaths, that I had no information about Doljani and Sovici at that time at all. I had heard nothing about that, and I can't give you an answer to anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand properly, in -- you did not in any way take part in the military operation that was conducted in -- in Sovici and Doljani.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In no way whatsoever. No way at all. And I have already told you the situations I was in and what role I played in those situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is something that I had noticed in your submissions. This is something you have told us already, but I just wanted to make quite sure. In April the military commander of the HVO was General Petkovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether my colleagues would like to put questions on Sovici and Doljani. No. General Praljak, we shall now look at the documents. I will first have a look at those documents which, according to you, are contested. You said these were forged documents. This has happened in a number of court cases, and the issue very often is raised. It seems incredible, but this is the case. So let's try and determine what the status of these forged documents is. I will ask the registrar to put this on the screen. P06937. That is the first one. Let me repeat -- well, there it is. The document has to be displayed in B/C/S, and we need to have the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask usher to help --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have it on my screen. Thank you. I have the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Registrar. The English translation is not the right one. The document in B/C/S is the right document, but the English translation is not the right document. There it is. So, Mr. Praljak, we have before us a document which is dated the 8th of November, which is the day when you left your job. There is a number here, 02-717/93, a file number. This document mentions a number of items that will completed afterwards. This document must have been used for other detainees when these detainees needed to conduct tasks outside. In what respect is this document a forged document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the 8th of November, I arrived at the Main Staff at 10.30 p.m. That's the earliest time I arrived probably, because after -- it was after the meeting in Tomislavgrad the previous day. I slept there, and then on the 8th of November I met up with General Roso in the afternoon and the whole evening to brief him on the situation. When I arrived, I signed two documents referring to the wounded, and -- and to reduce the time of the inquiry about Stupni Dol, an urgency note. And I would never have signed a document of this kind below Mijo Jelic. Now, B, I never sign my name is any document like this, this format and looking like this, never. There were documents -- a lot of documents that I saw here, but only on the document of the 8th when I wasn't there there's a forgery. And it says General Slobodan Praljak there. It should have said: "Pursuant to position received from the HVO Main Staff," and so on, "Slobodan Praljak," and then I would have signed it. So this is a forgery. I wasn't in Grude at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, before coming to work for this Tribunal, I specialised in forged documents. I had a whole series of cases of this kind. So this is a subject I'm quite familiar with. The document you have before you is a document that can be entirely forged. In other words, the entire document is forged, or part of the document is authentic, the part that relates to the 40 detainees, the signature of Mr. Jelic or his deputy, because you can see that there's a hyphen, so he may not have signed. And the forged part of the document would amount to your signature and the stamp. So the document could be authentic insofar as it mentions the 40 detainees, but your name has been added to the document. What do you think of this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't really say what isn't right with this document, whether it's 40 or not 40, whether it's Jelic's signature or not. I never signed a document like this. This was subsequently copied on a copier or copied my signature for who knows what reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is something you've told us already. General Praljak, your lawyers and their assistants, well, did you think of sending a letter? Mijo Jelic, did you think of sending him a letter? I don't know whether he's alive or not or dead. And among the evidence adduced you say that there are some forged documents. You could have asked him who added the stamp and the name of Slobodan Praljak. Is that something you did or something you didn't do, and if you didn't do it, why not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did not do that, nor will I do that. I don't want to try and justify myself since I wasn't there on the 8th. Mr. Petkovic knows that full well. You have the statement by Mr. Roso of how long I was with him, and so I can't sign under Mijo Jelic. It doesn't say "Authorised by" or what. Somebody just copied out something. So I don't want to justify this and justify myself. And somebody wants to put that in on the 8th. I don't want to defend myself by anything else but my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have some idea of who may have want you to endorse this document? Do you have no idea what so ever?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many people in this courtroom -- well, many documents have been forged, in the Blaskic trial, there are different services at work, fingers in the pie, for what reason I don't want to go into that, to bring me in here and to accuse me. Those are the reasons, both on the Muslim side there were those who were very happy. Of course, the Croats were happy when some Muslims were accused. The Serbs are happy when we're accused, and there were all sorts of things going on there in this regard, but it has nothing to do with me. Well, for heaven's sake, the last day, as we saw, was -- well, it was done and never when I toured the front lines, supervised them, I never met a prisoner digging, because everybody knew my position on that issue and this was done behind me back, perhaps, if it went on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall now look at the second document, P04131.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, it's file number 1, list number 1. Binder number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not the right document on the screen, the B/C/S document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps there was a misunderstanding. We withdrew the document from the information you wanted to receive about the possibly forged documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, why did you withdraw it, because the document is now an authentic document and no longer a forged one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which document are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For technical reasons. It was a technical error in internal communication among the team. There was a wrong number that was placed on the document that we considered, so we put that right the very next day, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move on to the next document, P02823. There it is. This is a very short document which should stem from you, but we can't see your signature. So this was probably sent by a packet switching system to Mr. Stojic. Mr. Praljak, why would this document dated as the 17th of June, 1993, be forged?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would never write "Urgent, urgent." I never panicked, so this double use of the word "urgent," "urgent, urgent," "hitno, hitno." And you have a document before my departure where I tell Blaskic and the others, "Don't write this 'urgent, urgent,' panic and so on. Just calm down, the situation isn't as bad as it looks." I would never use these two words, "Urgent, urgent." That's impossible. I would say when's the tank arriving, or send the tank quickly, but this "hitno, hitno," "urgent, urgent" is not something that I would have written, certainly not. And you can look at all my orders and see that for yourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may have noticed that this document was filed. Since this was filed on the 17th of June at 08.40 at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is possible. Well, I can't do any -- just guesswork and speculate, but I might have said ask Siljeg. Well, if I was up there. I'd have to look at the dates, check the dates out to see what happened with the tank, and then he could say "Urgent, urgent," or someone else. But this isn't my style. I did not write this. The changes in the words. Well, there's more of that example. It's not just one example that people use words to adapt to their style. This is not the way I communicated, not my style. I can't say more than that. I have no idea, to be quite frank. What tank?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What would have been the point of drafting a forged document, to help who, to try and cover what up, whether the person was in Rama or Prozor? I don't see what the point is, really. You don't either?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No reason, no reason at all, Your Honours. Well, the tanks are supposed to arrive. Had I written this, I would have said, "Bruno, what's happened to the tanks?" Because there had probably been information that they were being repaired because they broke down all the time. And so then -- not Petkovic would be asked but Stojic, because he was in charge of this repair shop where they were repaired. So I have nothing against this document, I just say it's not my style of document, not my style at all and no reason for it. As opposed to the previous document which was a forgery with a specific intent, I just say about this document that it's not my style, and I wouldn't have written it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So let's look at -- at the third and last document, P02280. This document has not been admitted. Irrespective of the fact that it has not been admitted, let's try and see why this may have been forged. This document stems from you. This document is addressed to Siljeg. There is a file number, and some military data is provided. What do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document has nothing whatsoever to do with me, absolutely nothing. This is not my style. This is not my handwriting. This is not my signature. I -- I have no clue what this is all about. These are two different handwritings. In the top part the different -- the handwriting is one, and then there is another. You've seen my handwriting. You don't even need an expert to say that this has absolutely nothing to do with me. I don't know who signed this. I can't say anything about the document apart from the fact that this is not my style, not my handwriting, not my signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is not dated.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Antonetti and other Judges, I really can't say anything on top of what I've already told you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There again, what was the point? Why was this directed at you, for what reason?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't answer this. Nothing. What somebody wanted, why didn't they put a date on the document? What does this mean everything is level? I really can't speculate. I know what the intent was behind the document that was issued on the 8th. The intention was for somebody to say, "You also did what we claim you did," which is not true. And as for this document I can't say anything. I can't see its purpose, I can't see it's intent at the time, nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I have a few follow-up questions for you. According to what the Judges have understood, the HVO archives were transferred to Zagreb. When there are forged document, documents could have been forged before the transfer or after the transfer. If the documents were forged before the transfer, this means that the people who have done this were involved with the units. If this was done after the transfer, this means that there is an operation on a greater scale, because the documents need to be input in the system of the Republic of Croatia. This then becomes much more complicated. I know that at some point you were looking after the archives. Can you tell us whether according to you this was done before the transfer or after?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Antonetti, what the Republic of Croatia has is not a proper archives. You call it archives. Unfortunately, this is not precisely that. The HVO documents were sitting for a long time after the war in Herzegovina, in Grude, Ljubuski -- I beg your pardon. Yes, in Grude. And there was no control over them. And then they were transferred to Split, and there was no control over them there. And then somebody loaded them onto a truck and delivered them to the Croatian archives. The Croatian archives filed the documents and stamped them with the stamp "received." Everybody, literally everybody, and you can check that you yourselves, Your Honours. For example, if you ask somebody from the Prosecutor's office who would then find somebody in Zagreb to take a certain number of documents, and they could do that anyway they wanted to and take them to the Croatian archives, and they could say, "This is what I had at home, and I am handing that over to you." They will receive the documents. They will stamp the documents, and already tomorrow you can go there and you can take the documents and say that you received them from the Croatian archives. This is how some documents were created there. This is a fact. And I know that. I know that some private individuals brought papers over there and left them there, and that's why we sought opinion from the director of the Croatian archives at the time. We wanted him to tell us exactly how he obtained documents. And these are not archival holdings, these are the holdings or documents that the archives received in one way or another. In the meantime, anybody could have injected anything that they wanted. They could have forged anything they wanted. They could have pulled out any document they wanted. And this is the truth, what I'm telling you. All the other accused here know that, and you also have a letter by Mr. Kolanovic. I believe that that's his name. I beg your pardon, it's a statement, yes. Mr. Kolanovic's statement as to the manner, how he received papers which are purported here to be from the archives of the -- of the Republic of Croatia. So these are not archival holdings. These are just papers which are safe-kept in the archives of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... why there were these forgeries, forged documents. We have nothing which may enable us to identify the authors of these forgeries. So, General Praljak, now we are going to examine the constitutional problems. My own working programme is the following: First of all, we'll see the Constitution of former Yugoslavia, after which we will see the Constitution of the Republic of Croatia and the Constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we will finish with the Constitution of the Croatian Community. The Constitution of former Yugoslavia is 1D02976, but I only need page 1D60-0579. Right. These are the basic principles. Could we also have it in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, Your Honours, I would kindly ask you for -- this previous document to be given to any handwriting expert to compare it with my own handwriting, and they will tell you that one has nothing whatsoever to do with the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, in the introduction or preamble of this Constitution, we read that there is a right for every nation to self-determination, which includes the right to secede. So it would seem that in the Constitution which was prevailing at the time over all the republics, it was acknowledged that there might be a self-rule or determination which could lead to a separation or a secession. This constitutional principle of Yugoslavia, was it well-understood and accepted by everyone?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not everybody accept this. The principle in question is the fundamental principle of Leninism, which means that peoples had the right -- and this is Lenin's doctrine, that every people has the right to self-determination until -- up to the secession from any other people. And since this Leninist principle was a dogma for communists, in the Constitution of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia and at this AVNOJ meeting, that principle was confirmed. In the second world war the parties were also divide. There was the Main Staff of the partisan movements of Croatia, Serbia, Kosovo and Metohija, and so on and so forth. At the same time, communists were convinced that they had resolved the ethnic problem by adopting a new form of organisation of society and that this particular right would never be evoked, but they never abolished it. They simply thought apart from the Brezhnev Doctrine of limited sovereignty, which he used to attack Czechoslovakia, that's when they introduced the doctrine of limited sovereignty, but this did not apply to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This constitutional principle, did it provide or make a possibility for the independence of Croatia towards the federal state or -- or was there a way which would allow an accession to independence towards separate republics even if the principle was a Leninist principle?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an absolute right. Further on the first paragraph continues to elaborate this. It says here, and I quote towards the end: "The working people, peoples and nationalities, shall realise their sovereign rights in the socialist republics and in the socialist autonomous provinces in keeping with their constitutional rights." Further on, and I continue: "In the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, when this is in the interests of everybody as established by this Constitution." The federation is a joint interest which may exist but doesn't have to exist. I have highlighted some other points, but I would not dwell upon them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... but as Mr. Karnavas says, we will progress step-by-step. Let's go to Article 57 at page 1D60-0639. Right. In the English version it starts by "Self-managing."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've got that, Your Honour. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Constitution of former Yugoslavia, one gets the impression that communities of interest were foreseen where people could in a certain way associate in a common interest. What do you think of it? This article, do you think it meant that it would be -- it could foreshadow an association of Croatian interests in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Can't one read within this article a sort of invitation to people to have a sort of self-rule?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. The lowest territorial unity was a local commune. It could be two streets, for example. In Zagreb I belonged to the local commune which had only two streets, and we were a local commune, and we were organised as such. We had our rights, and we also had our duties, and we could also team up with another local commune. And once we did that in order to resolve the issue of a stream that flew between our two local communes --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you will allow me and if you're really interested in this article, I would like to say that this article applies the so-called SIZ or self-managing communities of interest. And now that I've said that, I believe that General Praljak will be able to expand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a very complicated matter, and I am afraid that you will not be able to understand, because this falls under the theory of self-managing socialism as created by Kardelj and Suvar. It goes like this: Look at this suit that I'm wearing. And now, this suit consists of the manufacturer of the cloth, thread, buttons, lining, and different people manufacture all that. And this is their idea: What is sold at the end is the suit, and all the manufacturers will join up in the so-called self-managing community of interest because it is in their interest to produce the suit. And now how much money goes to each of them? How much money goes to the producers of buttons? It's not a market-based theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... despite counsel's invitation for the general to go down this road, I think it's not responsive to the President's question, and it also is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, what I was interested in with this Article 57 was a sort of spirit of the text which seemed to be inviting people to associate in interest communities -- communities of interest, and several associations or -- you spoke of the fact that in your street there was an association with another street. Now you say that it's rather complicated, just like a suit which can be made with several parts. I would like to have your point of view about the mentality, the mind of people in former Yugoslavia, whoever they are, Croatians, Serbs, Muslim. There was already in their mentality the possibility that they could associate not necessarily within a global state but in communities of specific interest as the Croatians did. Is this sort of affiliation which I'm trying to check, so I just wanted to ask you, General Praljak, this article in the Constitution, didn't it foreshadow what the Croatians between themselves were going to do later in Mostar, Livno, Ravno, and so on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only was it possible, it was even encouraged, Your Honours. This was encouraged. Different basis was used, and I did not use the example of a suit for no reason at all. They wanted to avoid the market economy approach. Everything else was encouraged. There were territorial associations. There was a cultural associations, and I'll know all that only to well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D60-0640. All this took a lot of time, so I say once again. Yes, just a moment. My colleague wishes to ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: As long as we still have it on the screen, I'm interested in the last subparagraph of Article 56 which in fact speaks about self-managing communities of a territorial nature. And if one reads this, that such communities may be set up for an area wider than the territory of a commune, that communities may be set up for the territories of several communes as part of this self-managing community of interest. One could come to the conclusion that that's exactly what HB, Herceg-Bosna, was, that Herceg-Bosna was a creation in application of the Constitution of the Federal Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia. What is your comment to this hypothesis?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, Your Honour Judge Trechsel. Not only were they able to but they were encouraged to form associations applying different principles in order to achieve a more efficient administration, in order to be able to solve different problems, in order to be able to produce a suit. Everybody was encouraged. Local communes, municipalities, everybody. You could have an association of municipalities which produced tobacco or wine or which wanted to organise some sports games. Association was allowed on any principle: Association of communes, municipalities, groups of municipalities, what have you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Within the same frame of mind, let's look at Article 59. This is 1D60-0640. Mr. Praljak, one gets the impression when reading this article 59 that these communities of interest may be set up, may constitute themselves, but this depends from a political and social assembly which should under certain conditions of procedure constitute rules, find solutions, and so on. So it wasn't possible overnight to decide to create a community. It had to follow certain rules, procedural rules. Is this true or not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. They would appoint their delegates, the delegates would create an assembly. They would have to have a Statute that would apply to their work. They would have to declare what they want to achieve, and they had to declare all that to the socialist alliance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are now going to stop, because there is another article I would like to study, Article 114, which I will already give to the registrar. The page, we will be able to see it tomorrow, it's 1D60-0673. Like that we can begin tomorrow afternoon. And I will still have a few articles of the Constitution to ask you questions about. The Yugoslav Constitution is a real monument. I have just highlighted certain articles. We could have spent hours on it, but I'm just mentioning those which are specifically interesting for the matter at hand. So it's nearly 7.00 p.m. I wish everyone a good evening and to read constitutional texts or constitutions tonight, and we will talk about it tomorrow. Thank you. The Chamber is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 17th day of June, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.
